video_title: How to Stop the Tragedy of the Commons with Iroro Tanshi | TGS 241
gist: Nigerian bat conservationist Iroro Tanshi (transcribed as 'Auroro Toni') explains how the rediscovery of the critically endangered short-tailed roundleaf bat, followed days later by a wildfire, led to a community-run 'zero wildfire' programme: a daily fire-danger signpost built on free NASA weather/fire data and enforced through village bylaws, with over 90% of farmers wanting to continue. She is now scaling it pantropically through a Tropical Fire Alliance, and argues that the Congo Basin is a more resilient carbon sink than the Amazon but gets only a fraction of its funding and capacity.

insights.claim: In the Nigerian forest landscape Tanshi works in, wildfires usually start on farms during land-clearing burns before spreading into forest, so the same fires destroy both bat habitat and neighbouring farmers' crops.
insights.speaker: Iroro Tanshi
insights.so_what: Conservation and farmer livelihoods share the same threat, which lines up their incentives.
insights.quote: the fires actually start on farms before they go through forest. And so they destroy other farms near them

insights.claim: Farmers burn crop residue because fire is a cheap way to clear land, returns some nutrients to the soil and reduces pest and fungal problems, even though its overall ecological effects are net negative.
insights.speaker: Iroro Tanshi
insights.so_what: Banning burning outright ignores real cost savings for farmers; managing when they burn works better.

insights.claim: Climate change has made rainfall timing unpredictable, with first rains sometimes slipping from March to April, so farmers can no longer rely on traditional knowledge of the safe time to burn. Communities framed this as both a climate problem and a data problem.
insights.speaker: Iroro Tanshi
insights.so_what: Local forecasting and decision tools are a direct climate-adaptation need in smallholder farming.
insights.quote: there's a climate change problem and then there's a data problem

insights.claim: The zero wildfire programme's core tool is a simple fire-danger signpost showing farmers each morning whether it is a good, medium-risk or bad day to burn, built from freely available NASA weather and fire data.
insights.speaker: Iroro Tanshi
insights.so_what: Simple, low-cost tools using free satellite data can change behaviour across a landscape.
insights.quote: you would see a signpost that says it's a good day to burn or a bad day to burn or a medium risk day

insights.claim: Communities chose on their own to enforce the fire-warning tool through their existing bylaws. One community punishes anyone whose fire spreads to another farm on a high-risk day with exile and a fine of about $5,000.
insights.speaker: Iroro Tanshi
insights.so_what: Rules that communities make and enforce themselves give a conservation programme real teeth.
insights.quote: you get exiled you pay like a $5,000 fine or so

insights.claim: Tanshi says the tragedy of the commons in landscape burning cannot be solved by uncoordinated individual efforts. Collective action works when it starts with careful listening, 'translating' what communities say, and building tools together with them.
insights.speaker: Iroro Tanshi
insights.so_what: Programmes that start by listening to communities and building tools with them work better than ones imposed from outside.
insights.quote: in terms of solving the tragedy of the commons it requires collective action

insights.claim: Communities enforce the fire rules because they want to protect their farms and food supply, not because they care about bats. Some villagers had lost their farms to fire years earlier and still depended on distant relatives to eat.
insights.speaker: Iroro Tanshi
insights.so_what: Conservation succeeds when it is presented in terms of livelihoods rather than species.
insights.quote: it's not because they really care about bats. I have to be honest with you

insights.claim: Annual surveys since the programme began show more than 90% of farmers want to keep using the fire-warning system.
insights.speaker: Iroro Tanshi
insights.so_what: Most farmers keep using the system, so it is likely to last beyond a single project.

insights.claim: A real unresolved risk is that worsening drought could leave so few safe-to-burn days that the system becomes unworkable for farmers. Tanshi has no answer yet beyond going back to the communities.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens / Iroro Tanshi
insights.so_what: Adaptation tools can stop working as the climate keeps changing, so they need a plan for when that happens.

themes.theme: Scaling to a pantropical fire alliance

insights.claim: Tanshi's organisation has launched a Tropical Fire Alliance and a tropical fire lab to take the community fire-prevention model to forests across the tropics. They are adapting it to local conditions such as drained peatlands in Indonesia and pasture and agroforestry systems in the Brazilian Amazon.
insights.speaker: Iroro Tanshi
insights.so_what: A model proven in one village is being turned into a platform for many countries.
insights.quote: we've now launched the tropical fire alliance

insights.claim: Tanshi estimates that at pantropical scale, preventing wildfires and letting fire-damaged areas recover could remove about 1 gigaton of carbon from the air.
insights.speaker: Iroro Tanshi
insights.so_what: Community fire prevention could become a large nature-based carbon lever.
insights.quote: we will really start to get about to about 1 gigatons of carbon out of the air

insights.claim: Tanshi says frontline communities, who suffer the most from climate impacts, are also doing the most about them, and that collective action with them pays off almost instantly.
insights.speaker: Iroro Tanshi
insights.so_what: Funding community-led adaptation may deliver results faster than top-down approaches.
insights.quote: the people who are doing the most are also the people who are actually experiencing the most

insights.claim: Tanshi says the Congo Basin appears to be a more resilient carbon sink than the Amazon. It still absorbs a lot of carbon despite facing the highest rate of deforestation, and the reasons are not yet understood.
insights.speaker: Iroro Tanshi
insights.so_what: The world may be underestimating, and underprotecting, the carbon sink that is holding up better.
insights.quote: the Congo basin appears to be much more resilient at being a carbon sink than the Amazon forest

insights.claim: Tanshi warns that, like the passenger pigeon, a system that looks stable such as the Congo Basin carbon sink can decline steeply once it passes a critical threshold if nothing is done.
insights.speaker: Iroro Tanshi
insights.so_what: Apparent stability is no reason to postpone investment, because collapse can be nonlinear.

insights.claim: Tanshi says the Congo Basin receives only a fraction of the finance, local scientific capacity and institutional support that the Amazon gets. Efforts such as the Congo Basin Science Initiative are trying to close that gap.
insights.speaker: Iroro Tanshi
insights.so_what: Money and capacity for African forest protection lag far behind the need.

insights.claim: About one in five mammal species is a bat (over 1,500 of roughly 6,000 mammal species). Nigeria holds about one-third of Africa's bat species because of its wide range of habitat types.
insights.speaker: Iroro Tanshi
insights.so_what: Nigeria is a hotspot for a large, understudied group of mammals.
insights.quote: Nigeria holds about onethird of the number of species you find across the continent

insights.claim: Bats disperse the seeds of the shea tree across the landscape, so most shea butter used in cosmetics comes from bat-planted trees; managed shea production systems are a recent development of roughly the past decade.
insights.speaker: Iroro Tanshi
insights.so_what: Supply chains for cosmetics ingredients quietly depend on bats.

insights.claim: Bats pollinate Parkia biglobosa, a savannah tree whose flowers are fertile for a single night and whose fermented seeds are a staple spice across West Africa.
insights.speaker: Iroro Tanshi
insights.so_what: A staple West African food spice depends on bats for pollination.

insights.claim: Rising heat is already stressing bats. They fan themselves to cool down, which costs energy, and in places like India bats are falling out of trees from heat stroke, so cities may stop being viable habitat for urban pollinating bats.
insights.speaker: Iroro Tanshi
insights.so_what: Pollination in urban gardens and nearby farms may decline as cities heat up.
insights.quote: we're crying about insects. We're going to start crying about bats soon

insights.claim: Tanshi says Nigerian forests are near 1.5°C of warming, cities are hotter still, and intact natural areas will increasingly serve as thermal refuges for wildlife.
insights.speaker: Iroro Tanshi
insights.so_what: Protecting standing forest also protects places where wildlife can escape the heat.

insights.claim: Most Nigerians believe bats are witches, yet the same people may eat other bat species. Rural forest communities relate to nature in spiritual and ancestral terms, while city dwellers show little concern for biodiversity.
insights.speaker: Iroro Tanshi
insights.so_what: Conservation messages need tailoring to local beliefs and to rural versus urban audiences.
insights.quote: the vast majority of people think bats are witches

insights.claim: Tanshi says pangolins are the most trafficked mammal, but in Africa much of that trade starts with hunters taking them for local food, which makes it a different problem from the usual trafficking story.
insights.speaker: Iroro Tanshi
insights.so_what: Measures against pangolin trafficking need to address local hunting for food, not just international smuggling.
